Nonmetric asymmetric MDS by the radius-distance (circle) model

Source: R/circle_mds.R
circle_mds.Rd

Each object j is a point x_j in a p-dimensional Euclidean space with a circle (sphere, hypersphere) of radius r_j centered at it. The asymmetric proximity from j to k is represented by m_jk = d_jk - r_j + r_k, the distance from the near edge of the circle of j to the far edge of the circle of k, which is assumed to be monotonically decreasing in similarities (increasing in dissimilarities). The fit is measured by S = sqrt(sum((m_jk - mhat_jk)^2) / sum((m_jk - mbar)^2)) (Kruskal's stress formula 2 applied to m_jk), where mhat_jk are the disparities obtained by monotone regression (primary approach to ties). S is minimized over the coordinates and radii.

Usage

circle_mds(
  x,
  ndim = 2,
  type = c("similarity", "dissimilarity"),
  ndim_max = ndim,
  nrandom = 10,
  maxit = 1000,
  reltol = 1e-10,
  seed = 1,
  kappa = 10
)

Arguments

x

A square matrix of asymmetric proximities, or a list of such matrices (one per source) for the two-mode three-way model. The diagonal is ignored; other missing cells are left out of the fit.

ndim

Number of dimensions.

type

"similarity" (default) or "dissimilarity". If x has a type attribute set by as_proximity(), that is used.

ndim_max

Dimensionality at which the rational initial configuration is built; the solutions are reduced from there down to ndim.

nrandom

Number of random starts tried in addition to the rational start (0 uses the rational start only).

maxit, reltol

Passed to stats::optim().

seed

Random seed for the random starts. The state of the random number generator is restored afterwards. NULL uses (and advances) the current state of the generator.

kappa

Two-mode three-way model only: the upper bound of the ratio of the longest to the shortest semiaxis of the ellipses of a source (max_t u_it / min_t u_it). Without it the ellipses can collapse to line segments while the radii diverge. A warning is given when a solution reaches the bound.

Value

An object of class c("mdspace_circle", "mdspace") with conf (n x ndim), radius, stress (S), niter (gradient evaluations of the chosen solution), mjk and disparity (n x n matrices, NA on the diagonal and missing cells), path (S at each dimensionality from ndim_max to ndim for the rational start), starts (S of each start, the rational one first), best_start (which start was chosen), and converged.

Details

The initial configuration is "rational" as in Okada and Imaizumi (1987): Torgerson's method applied to the symmetrized dissimilarities, with the additive constant that makes them Euclidean (Cailliez, 1983, as in stats::cmdscale() with add = TRUE; Okada & Imaizumi, 1997, add Torgerson's constant), gives the configuration in ndim_max dimensions, and the least squares solution of r_k - r_j = a_jk (a_jk the skew-symmetric part of the dissimilarities) gives the radii. The solution in ndim_max dimensions is then reduced one dimension at a time by its principal axes down to ndim. Because the radius-distance model has local minima, nrandom random starts (10 by default) are also tried in ndim dimensions and the solution with the smallest S is returned (Okada & Imaizumi, 2024, Section 4.1.1).

With few objects the solution may not be unique: a simulation with n = 5 (20 off-diagonal cells) reached S = 0 even with error while the coordinates differed from the true ones by up to 0.8 (normalized scale), and one case with n = 10 in three dimensions did the same. The configuration should then be interpreted with care. See develop/20261117_circle_recovery.R in the source repository.

The solution is normalized so that the configuration is centered with the sum of squared coordinates equal to n, and the smallest radius is 0 (the radii are determined only up to an additive constant), as in the nASYMS program.

Two-mode three-way model. When x is a list of N matrices (sources), the model of Okada and Imaizumi (1997) is fitted: a common configuration of points and circles, a symmetry weight w_i and asymmetry weights u_it for each source. In source i the circle of object j becomes an ellipse with semiaxes u_it r_j, and m_jki = w_i d_jk - v_jki (r_j - r_k) with v_jki = w_i d_jk / sqrt(sum_t ((x_jt - x_kt) / u_it)^2). S = sqrt(mean_i S_i^2), where S_i is stress formula 2 within source i. The asymmetry weights are fixed to have geometric mean 1 over all sources and dimensions (they and the radii are otherwise determined only up to reciprocal scaling), the aspect ratio of each source is bounded by kappa, and the problem is solved by L-BFGS-B. w_i does not affect S and is set afterwards so that sum_jk (m_jki - mbar_i)^2 = n, as in the original paper and nASYMS. The initial configuration is the Torgerson solution (with the additive constant) of the mean of the symmetrized dissimilarities; when reducing from ndim_max, the dimensions with the smallest contribution are dropped. The result additionally has weights (data frame with w and u1, u2, ...), aspect, stress_source and at_bound.

The minimization uses the analytic gradient of S with the disparities held fixed, which is the gradient of S as a function of the coordinates and radii (Kruskal, 1964b), and stats::optim() (BFGS) instead of the steepest descent of the original program.

References

Okada, A., & Imaizumi, T. (1987). Nonmetric multidimensional scaling of asymmetric proximities. Behaviormetrika, 14(21), 81-96.

Okada, A., & Imaizumi, T. (2024). Applied multidimensional scaling of asymmetric relationships. Springer.

Cailliez, F. (1983). The analytical solution of the additive constant problem. Psychometrika, 48(2), 305-308.

Okada, A., & Imaizumi, T. (1997). Asymmetric multidimensional scaling of two-mode three-way proximities. Journal of Classification, 14, 195-224.

Kruskal, J. B. (1964b). Nonmetric multidimensional scaling: A numerical method. Psychometrika, 29(2), 115-129.

Examples

x <- matrix(c(NA, 5, 2, 1,
              3, NA, 4, 2,
              1, 2, NA, 6,
              2, 1, 4, NA), 4, byrow = TRUE)
fit <- circle_mds(x, ndim = 1)
fit
#> mdspace: circle 
#> Call: circle_mds(x = x, ndim = 1)
#> Objects: 4  Dimensions: 1 
#> Stress: 0.1915 
#> Iterations: 16 
#> Starts: 11 (rational + 10 random); best = random 8, S range 0.1915 to 0.6396
